Blessings and Passages for Torah Study justifying prayer in place of sacrificial offerings in the Italian rite

tei:bibl.tei:title: ברכות לתלמוד תורה לפני תפלה
Blessings and Passages for Torah Study justifying prayer in place of sacrificial offerings in the Italian rite
tei:bibl.tei:note: Converted from the export of opensiddur.org at 624215eef0.

tei:div.tei:p: The nusaḥ Italki (Italian rite) preserves a full curriculum of Torah study in advance of the morning prayers. Included are passages from the Torah, Mishnah, and Gemarah familiar to other nusḥaot. In the Italian rite, the blessings over Torah study and ensuing passages appear after all the other birkhot hashaḥar, concluding it and providing a bridge to liturgy preceding the Zemirot (a/k/a Pesuqei d’Zimra). What is remarkable in this tradition is how interlinked the blessing and recitation of these passages is to the otherwise separate and adjacent section concerning the sacrificial offerings in the Temple and the rules of halakhic exegesis in Rabbinic hermeneutics. While additional portions and verses are presented, the passages provide an explicit justification for the otherwise radical innovation carried forth in rabbinic Judaism to offer services of prayer in place of the services of the Temple cult, providing Hosea 14:3 as the authority to do so — a necessity in an age where the Torah mandated arrangements of animal sacrifices, incense and grain offerings, and wine libations remains otherwise interrupted.

This is the form of the blessing over studying Torah and the arrangement of daily Torah study in the Italian nusaḥ attested by Rabbi David Prato from his siddur, תפלה לדוד Preghiere di Rito Italiano (1949), pp. 12-25. Aside from the blessings, there is little Italian to accompany the rest of the text and so we have here included only English translations of the same. The English translations for the blessings, mainly follow the suggestion of Rabbi Prato’s Italian, where they exist. For the other passages (left untranslated by Rabbi Prato), we have adapted our translation from a variety of sources on Sefaria, choosing Everett Fox’s and Joshua Kulp’s translations where available. –Aharon Varady
